30-Day Digital Skills Challenge: Learn a Money-Making Skill From Scratch

A free, ebook-length teaching guide: choose one digital skill, set up your phone or laptop, follow a clear mission for each of 30 days, build a portfolio with no clients, then find your first people to pay you. Scripts, pricing, scam warnings and a one-page plan included.

By Princess Immanuel · Founder, Her Digital Playbook

Come and sit beside me, love, because I want to teach you something the way I would teach my own little sister: slowly, plainly, from the very beginning, with nothing skipped and no big words left unexplained.

Here is the idea. In the next thirty days, you are going to learn one digital skill, from absolute zero, and finish with a real piece of work you can show another human being. Not ten skills. Not "a bit of everything." One. By day thirty, you will not just have read about a money-making skill. You will have practised it every day, made something with it, and written down exactly how you would offer it to someone who might pay.

I want to be honest with you from the first page, babe. I cannot promise you income. Nobody honest can. What I can promise is a clear path, one small job per day, and a finished piece of proof at the end. Whether that turns into money, and how fast, depends on the skill you choose, the effort you give it and the people you reach out to. Some people find their first paying client within weeks of finishing something like this. Others take a few months. Both are normal.

You do not need a laptop to begin. A phone will carry you through a lot of this guide, and I will tell you clearly when a laptop would make a particular day easier. You do not need money to begin either. Everything we use in the first thirty days has a free option.

Here is what this guide covers, so you can see the whole road before we walk it:

  • What a digital skill actually is, and why it matters for your income.
  • How to choose your one skill in a calm, sensible way.
  • How to set up your phone or laptop, your learning space and your daily time.
  • A full thirty-day plan, one small mission per day, with a clear finish line each day.
  • How to build a portfolio piece, even if you have never had a client.
  • Where to go to be found, platform by platform, with scripts you can copy.
  • Cold email, message and call scripts, and how to use them kindly and legally.
  • A full plan for turning your skill into income, with honest numbers to think about.
  • Common mistakes, a troubleshooting table, scam warnings, twelve questions, a checklist and a one-page plan.

One more thing before we begin. Please do not try to read this whole guide in one sitting and then feel behind. It is a long guide because I want to leave nothing out, not because you must do everything at once. Read a chapter, do the work for that chapter, and come back tomorrow. Slow and steady is not a weakness here. It is the method.

One skill, thirty days, one finished piece of proof.

1What A Digital Skill Really Is

Let us start from absolute zero, the way I promised.

A skill is something you can do well enough that another person would rather pay you to do it than do it themselves. Cooking is a skill. Braiding hair is a skill. Sewing is a skill. Explaining a hard subject to a child is a skill.

A digital skill is simply a skill you do using a phone, a computer and the internet. The work happens on a screen, and the result is something that can be sent over the internet: a document, a design, a video, a spreadsheet, a piece of writing, a website, a set of organised emails.

That last part matters, so let me say it again. Because digital work can be sent over the internet, it does not care where you live. A person in Lagos, Manchester, Toronto or Nairobi can do the same design job for the same client. This is why digital skills are so powerful for women who want flexibility: the work can fit around your life, your family, your studies or your current job.

Digital skill is not the same as "being techy"

I want to remove a fear right now. Many women tell me, "I am not a tech person." Love, you do not need to be. Using a digital skill is not the same as understanding how a computer works inside. You do not need to know how a car engine works to drive to the market. Most digital skills are simply tools you learn to use well, the way you learned to use a phone.

You also do not need to be good at maths, or good at drawing, or good at public speaking. Different skills ask different things of you. Some need a good eye. Some need clear writing. Some need patience and tidiness. Some need a friendly voice. Part of this guide is helping you find the one that fits you.

Skills versus jobs versus businesses

Three words people mix up, so let us separate them:

  • A skill is what you can do (for example, designing a flyer).
  • A job is when one employer pays you regularly to use your skill for them.
  • A business (or freelancing) is when you sell your skill to several people, usually one project at a time.

This challenge builds the first thing: the skill. Once you have a skill and some proof, you can choose whether to look for a job, freelance, or both. We will talk about all three later.

A few examples of digital skills

Here are some that beginners can start learning with free tools. I am not recommending all of them. I am simply showing you the range so you can see what is out there:

SkillWhat you actually doWhat you produce
Graphic designArrange text, images and colours so something looks clear and attractiveFlyers, social posts, simple logos
Social media managementPlan and schedule posts, reply to comments, keep a page activeA posting calendar, scheduled posts
CopywritingWrite words that help someone understand and buyProduct descriptions, short emails, captions
Virtual assistanceHandle admin tasks like inboxes, calendars and organising filesAn organised system for a busy person
Video editingCut and arrange video clips, add captions and soundShort videos for social media
Data entry and spreadsheetsOrganise information accurately in rows and columnsClean, usable spreadsheets
Canva template designBuild reusable designs others can editTemplates for posts, CVs, planners
Basic website buildingPut pages together using a simple website builderA small business website
Transcription and captioningTurn spoken audio into accurate textTranscripts and subtitles
Online tutoring or teachingExplain a subject clearly over video or chatLessons or worksheets

Notice that every single row ends with something you produce. That is the key. A skill becomes real when it leaves a visible result behind.

Big Sis Note 💖 Big Sis Note: You do not have to pick the skill that sounds most impressive. Pick the one you can imagine doing on a rainy Tuesday when you do not feel like it. That is the one you will actually finish.

2Why Learning One Skill Beats Learning Ten

Before we choose, I need to talk about the biggest trap in this whole area, because it catches almost every beginner.

It is called skill hopping. On Monday you watch a video about graphic design. On Tuesday you see someone earning from video editing and you switch. On Thursday a friend mentions copywriting and you open a new tab. By the end of the month you have watched forty videos and can do nothing well.

Here is why this happens, in simple terms. Your brain learns a skill through repetition and small mistakes. The first time you try to design a flyer, it looks awful. The fifth time, it looks better. The twentieth time, it looks good. If you restart every week, you never reach the twentieth time. You stay at the awful stage over and over, and you start to believe you are "just not good at this."

You are not bad at it. You simply have not stayed long enough to find out.

What changes when you commit to one

  • Each day builds on the last one, so you improve visibly.
  • You can finish something, which gives you real confidence.
  • You can show a person a finished piece instead of saying "I am learning."
  • You can describe your skill in one clear sentence, which makes it easier for someone to hire you.

Take Adaora, a made-up example. Adaora is twenty-six and works in a shop. Over three months she "tried" graphic design, video editing, writing and social media, a few evenings each. She felt exhausted and told herself she had no talent. Now imagine a second version of her, also made up, who chose Canva design and did it for thirty days. By the end she has twelve small designs, a tidy little portfolio and a simple message she can send to local businesses. Same woman, same free time, completely different result. The only difference was choosing one thing.

And choosing one thing does not trap you forever. After thirty days you can add a second skill, switch, or deepen the first. The point is to finish one thing first.

Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Treating the first week as a "test drive" of several skills. Test-driving is what Chapter three is for, and it takes one afternoon, not a week.

3Choose Your One Skill Without Overthinking

This is the chapter where many people get stuck for weeks, so let me give you a simple method that takes about an hour. We will use four questions and one tiebreaker.

Question one: What do you already do without being asked?

Look at your life for clues. Do you naturally organise things for friends? You may suit virtual assistance. Do people ask you to fix their CVs or captions? You may suit writing. Do you enjoy making things look neat and pretty? Design may fit you. Do you like watching and re-watching videos and noticing how they are cut? Video editing may call you.

Write down three things people already ask you for help with. They are clues, not rules.

Question two: Which of these would you tolerate for an hour a day?

Not love. Tolerate. Passion is lovely but it is not required. You are not looking for a soulmate. You are looking for something you do not hate on a bad day. Try imagining yourself doing it for an hour tomorrow and ask, "Could I sit with this?"

Question three: Can you learn it with what you have?

Some skills need a strong laptop. Some need only a phone. Be honest about your tools. If you only have a phone, favour skills like social media management, copywriting, simple Canva design, transcription or virtual assistance. If you have a laptop, more doors open, like video editing and website building.

Question four: Do real people pay for it?

You can check this in ten minutes without spending a penny. Search a job or freelance site for the skill name and see whether people are asking for it. Look at how many requests there are and what they actually ask for. Do not worry about the exact prices yet. You are only checking that the demand exists. (Platforms change, so please check what is available where you live.)

The tiebreaker: the one-afternoon test

If you are torn between two skills, spend one afternoon on each. Not one week. Follow a free beginner tutorial for ninety minutes and make one tiny thing. Afterwards, ask yourself:

  • Did time pass quickly or slowly?
  • Was I curious about what came next?
  • Did I feel stupid in a useful way (learning) or stupid in a miserable way (dread)?

Choose the one that felt more like curiosity. Done. No more research.

Using the chart to decide

QuestionSkill ASkill B
Do people already ask me for this?
Could I do it for an hour a day?
Can I learn it with my phone or laptop?
Is there visible demand?
Which one felt like curiosity in the afternoon test?

Fill it in honestly. The skill with more ticks wins. If it is a tie, pick the one whose finished result you would be proud to show your mother.

Coffee Break ☕ Coffee Break: If you have spent more than a week choosing, you are not being careful, you are avoiding starting. Pick the best one on your list today. A decent choice you actually begin beats a perfect choice you never open.
